planting.note: Plant small nursery-grown specimens into a crevice or raised scree bed where the crown sits above grade and water drains away instantly after rain.

directions: This Western Carpathian endemic grows wild only on limestone and dolomite cliffs in Slovakia, and it carries that lime-loving, sharply-drained preference straight into cultivation, forming a tight, woody hummock of narrow, glossy evergreen leaves barely rising above the surrounding scree. In late spring it studs itself with small, intensely fragrant rosy-pink flower clusters that are disproportionately showy for the plant's miniature size. Grow it in a trough, raised bed, or rock garden crevice with gritty, alkaline, humus-poor soil, and resist the urge to feed or water it generously, since lush conditions shorten its life. It resents root disturbance once settled, so choose a permanent site and top-dress with fresh grit each spring rather than transplanting.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered spot with reliable winter drainage, since this Mediterranean species is markedly less cold-tolerant than most garden daphnes and dislikes wet, frozen roots.

directions: Native to the mountains of southern Italy and parts of Turkey, this daphne forms a dense, rounded mound of small, leathery, dark green leaves with a soft gray-green underside, giving the whole shrub a two-toned shimmer in a breeze. Clusters of rosy-lilac, sweetly fragrant flowers open at the branch tips in mid to late spring and can repeat lightly later in the season. Give it well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil and light afternoon shade in hot climates, since it is more heat-tolerant than many alpine daphnes but still resents waterlogged roots. It is a good choice for a sheltered shrub border or large rock garden in milder zones where winter wet rather than cold is the main hazard, and like other daphnes it is best left undisturbed once planted.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in deep, well-drained soil on a sunny slope, training vines low and open to catch reflected heat the way growers on the island of Šolta traditionally do.

directions: Dobričić is an old Croatian red grape native to the island of Šolta, grown today mainly for its historic role as one of the two parents, alongside Crljenak Kaštelanski, of Plavac Mali, Dalmatia's signature red wine grape. On its own it yields lighter-colored, softer-tannin wine than its famous offspring, and it is now rare enough that most remaining vines are maintained in old island plots or heritage collections rather than large commercial blocks. Grow it on free-draining, stony soil in full sun, since the variety is adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean island conditions and performs poorly in damp or shaded sites. Prune to an open, low framework for good air movement, and expect modest yields of small, thick-skinned clusters that ripen in early to mid autumn.
